payload.question_text: Which statements describe image classification? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Correct. Image classification predicts one text label for the image's main subject.

options.text: It identifies an image's main subject
options.rationale: Correct. The predicted label identifies the image's main subject.

options.text: It marks each object with a box

options.rationale: Not quite. Marking several objects with rectangular locations is object detection.
options.better_fit: Choose this when multiple objects and their bounding-box locations are needed.

feedback.instructional: Image classification predicts one main-subject label. Object detection finds objects and their locations.

options.text: It uses many labeled training images

payload.question_text: Which technique can interpret objects and activities in an image, then generate a description?

options.error_type: confuses an image description with one label

options.better_fit: Choose this when the result needed is one label, such as a fruit type.

options.better_fit: Choose this when exact pixels belonging to each object are required.

options.text: It predicts only one image label

evaluation_context.goal: Produce an excellent, source-faithful learner session while preserving all deterministic correctness, identity, and sequence constraints.
evaluation_context.source_fidelity_goal: Independently verify the hard-gated edited challenger against the supplied source material. Reject unsupported facts, answers, explanations, feedback, or terminology changes; do not edit the artifact.

criteria.factual_fidelity: Every claim and answer is faithful to the supplied source.

sources.location: sources/5. Introduction to computer vision concepts.md

evidence.statement: The keyed answers and explanations consistently match the supplied definitions of image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, contextual image analysis, multimodal models, and computer vision.
Single-choice and true/false items have one defensible key; multi-select items explicitly identify all source-supported statements, such as one label plus labeled training images for classification.
Distractors are adjacent techniques from the same domain and are distinguished by output type: one label, boxes, pixels, or descriptions.

Incorrect options are explicitly mapped to realistic confusions, including classification versus detection, detection versus segmentation, image description versus object location, and multimodal versus image-only processing.

The ordered sequence begins with narrow classification and contextual questions before establishing the broader computer-vision category, then revisits concepts in paired recall and true/false checks without a clear progression to workplace application.
The exact sequence follows a rigid repeating pattern of two multiple-choice items followed by two true/false items three times, making the interaction highly predictable.

Prompt forms vary between definition questions, technique-identification questions, multi-select stems, and declarative true/false statements, but several stems use repeated 'Which...' wording and the true/false items are formulaically phrased.
The stated SLO targets simple workplace image tasks, but most questions are abstract definitions; workplace context appears mainly in feedback rather than in the learner-facing prompts.
Incorrect-answer feedback generally names the misconception, contrasts the governing output types, and gives a better-fit condition; item explanations reinforce the keyed concept.

The Level 1 session uses mostly Remembering and Understanding items, which fits an introductory unit, but the low cognitive demand and repeated direct definitions provide limited challenge by the end.
The artifact consistently distinguishes labels, bounding boxes, pixel classification, descriptions or tags, visual input, and multimodal image-text combinations in line with the source.
The artifact is accurate and well-scaffolded at the individual-item level, but the full sequence is predictable, definition-heavy, and only weakly connected to the stated workplace-task objective.

critical_defects.summary: The ordered session does not build from the broad computer-vision concept to technique distinctions and then workplace application; it starts with narrow concepts and cycles through repeated recall checks.

evidence.statement: Items 0-1 test individual techniques before item 9 defines computer vision, while items 2-3, 6-7, and 10-11 repeat the same concepts as true/false checks rather than advancing the learner toward task selection.

largest_gap.summary: The exact sequence uses a rigid MC, MC, true/false, true/false cycle and repeats each concept family in the same pattern, reducing engagement and making response mechanics predictable.

evidence.statement: The 12-item order is three consecutive repetitions of two multiple-choice items followed by two true/false items, with paired rung-1 and rung-2 checks for the same concepts.

largest_gap.repair_instruction: Re-sequence and selectively replace or convert the repeated checks so the session alternates mechanics naturally and ends with scenario-based technique selection; preserve the existing source-backed concepts and deterministic item identities.

result.concise_summary: Source fidelity, answer keys, terminology, distractors, and feedback are strong, with no evident deterministic correctness or identity failure. The main weakness is the exact sequence: it is rigidly patterned, definition-heavy, and weakly aligned to the workplace-task SLO. Confidence is reduced because no approved references were supplied.
